I finally realized why I just can't get into The Sims 4, but I still find myself watching videos about The Sims 1.

For the longest time I thought it was just nostalgia. Like I was becoming one of those grumpy old-school fans who always says, "everything was better back then." But I don't think that's it anymore.

The Sims 1 wasn't just a life simulator. It was a satire of everyday life. As a kid, I completely missed that. The game constantly made fun of people's greed, stupidity, relationships, and everyday habits. It was full of dark humor, absurd situations, and it always felt like the developers didn't take themselves too seriously.

Then the series gradually became "safer." The Sims 4 is beautiful, polished, and has great build mode and Create-a-Sim. But it also feels... sterile. Like it lost the sharp, sarcastic personality that made the earlier games so memorable. Everything feels designed to avoid offending anyone, and somewhere along the way the series lost part of its soul.

I guess that's why I won't be coming back to The Sims 4. A building simulator with overly nice Sims just isn't what I'm looking for.

# The Sims 4 Review – Great Foundation, But It Feels Incomplete

## My Experience

I recently gave The Sims 4 another chance after not enjoying my first playthrough. While there are things I genuinely like about the game, there are also several issues that made it difficult to stay invested. After around 16 hours of gameplay, I found myself becoming bored and frustrated, despite wanting to enjoy the game.

As someone who grew up playing Sims games and even the free mobile version, I expected The Sims 4 to feel like the ultimate Sims experience. Instead, it often feels like I'm only getting a small slice of the game unless I'm willing to spend large amounts of money on DLC.

---

## What I Like

### Build Mode

The build mode is easily one of the strongest parts of The Sims 4.

* Building houses is fun and creative.
* There is a lot of freedom when designing rooms and layouts.
* Decorating homes can be very satisfying.
* The game allows players to create entire neighborhoods and communities.

However, some tools could be improved. Rotating and placing staircases can sometimes be awkward, especially for new players.

What I wish:
Adding multiplayer would build a community, talk to friends, visit each other, make relationship and show off! Socialising with other players would make this more lifelike!
---

## Important Advice for New Players

One of the biggest mistakes I made during my first playthrough was creating only a single household.

I strongly recommend:

* Creating multiple families.
* Building several homes before starting.
* Populating the neighborhood with your own Sims.
* Increasing household variety to make the world feel alive.

My first save became boring because there was only one family to interact with. Once I started filling the world with more Sims, the experience improved significantly, maybe addd recomandations for building more homes, or workplaces like gym, park and such, since I began doing it by staring over again, but was a bit hard to lear…

I have been a Simmer since the 4th grade, when I started with The Sims 2. I wasn't a big fan of The Sims 4 at first, at it was released with bare bones. The original game was supposed to be multiplayer, but that aspect of the game was scrapped last minute, resulting in a lackluster game at launch. It has been over a decade now since the launch of The Sims 4 and it has improved substantially. However, not enough. Compared to previous games in the series, The Sims 4 just falls short. I think part of this is due to the rough start the game had and partly due to the greed of EA. If you were to buy all of the DLC for this game, you would be spending over a grand. I wouldn't mind this if the DLC was worth the price. In previous Sims games, you got more value for your buck. Now, you only get about half of what you used to get and sometimes its just recolors or retextured. I will forever love this game (I also have a Sims related tattoo), but I don't think my loyalty will be forever, especially now that Paralives has released and has proved it can do just as well, or even better, than EA at including content and features in early access. 

There is also a troubling part to this story that has developed recently: The EA Buyout. While it hasn't gone through yet, it is still worrisome. If this deal goes through, it will be a deal breaker for me and I will no longer support The Sims. It's hard for me to give up a game I have loved for most of my life...but the franchise will no longer align with my beliefs if this buyout happens. I will fight for The Sims until then and I hope that in the future, EA will care about their customers and fan base.

**Recommended? Yes... but with a huge asterisk.**

I've played The Sims since the original game back in 2000, and after over 900 hours in The Sims 4, it's safe to say I genuinely love this franchise. I play heavily modded, own a large portion of the DLC, and when everything is working, there really is no other life simulation game that scratches the same itch.

The build mode is fantastic, Create-a-Sim is the best it's ever been, and the amount of creativity the game allows is incredible. I've spent countless hours building homes, creating generations of families, and telling stories that no other game lets me tell in quite the same way.

That said, loving The Sims 4 sometimes feels like being in a toxic relationship.

EA's DLC model is honestly ridiculous. Expansion packs routinely launch at around £40, yet many arrive with bugs, missing features, or gameplay systems that feel unfinished. The amount of money required to experience what many players would consider the "full game" is staggering. At this point, the combined DLC cost is enough to buy several AAA games.

Even more frustrating is that some features locked behind paid packs feel like things that should have been included in the base game years ago. Instead of meaningful expansions, there are times when content feels sliced up and sold separately.

The game is also plagued by bugs. Sims ignore commands, pathfinding breaks, packs interfere with each other, and new updates often seem to introduce as many problems as they fix. Long-time players have learned to expect bugs rather than be surprised by them.

I [b] genuinely [/b] tried to give this game a fair chance.

I grew up with The Sims 2 and The Sims 3, so I already knew about most of the criticism surrounding this game when it released back in 2014, but I still wanted to experience it for myself before judging it. After finally putting time into it years later, I understand exactly why so many longtime players feel disappointed.

The Sims 4 is probably the most aesthetically polished game in the franchise, and that is unfortunately where most of the praise ends for me.

There ARE aspects of the game that initially look appealing. The graphics are clean, the art style aged decently, and the Create-A-Sim system is accessible enough for casual players to immediately have fun with.

But the deeper you get into the game, the more restrictive everything starts to feel.

Even the build mode people constantly praise begins falling apart the second you want to create something beyond the game’s carefully limited systems. Suddenly you need cheats, debug menus, TOOL mod, Better BuildBuy, custom content, and twenty browser tabs open just to make the game feel flexible enough to properly express creativity.

And that becomes the core issue with The Sims 4 as a whole: so much of the experience depends on outside labor from the community instead of the actual game itself.

At some point you realize most of the best Sims 4 content is not even made by EA. The community fixes bugs EA ignores for years. Modders add more meaningful gameplay depth than official expansions. Custom content creators carry the game’s aesthetic variety almost entirely on their backs.

A life simulation game should not require this much external effort just to feel complete, immersive, or creatively satisfying.

Underneath the pretty graphics and smooth build mode is a life simulation game that feels incredibly shallow compared to its predecessors. The Sims 2 had insane attention to detail, personality, charm, and little interactions that made sims feel al…

Its Probably my favorite game next to a couple others. I love picking mods from Off sites and playing with the different DLCs, as an animal lover my favorite is definitely Cats & Dogs.

**Recommended? Yes... but with a huge asterisk.**

I've played The Sims since the original game back in 2000, and after over 900 hours in The Sims 4, it's safe to say I genuinely love this franchise. I play heavily modded, own a large portion of the DLC, and when everything is working, there really is no other life simulation game that scratches the same itch.

The build mode is fantastic, Create-a-Sim is the best it's ever been, and the amount of creativity the game allows is incredible. I've spent countless hours building homes, creating generations of families, and telling stories that no other game lets me tell in quite the same way.

That said, loving The Sims 4 sometimes feels like being in a toxic relationship.

EA's DLC model is honestly ridiculous. Expansion packs routinely launch at around £40, yet many arrive with bugs, missing features, or gameplay systems that feel unfinished. The amount of money required to experience what many players would consider the "full game" is staggering. At this point, the combined DLC cost is enough to buy several AAA games.

Even more frustrating is that some features locked behind paid packs feel like things that should have been included in the base game years ago. Instead of meaningful expansions, there are times when content feels sliced up and sold separately.

The game is also plagued by bugs. Sims ignore commands, pathfinding breaks, packs interfere with each other, and new updates often seem to introduce as many problems as they fix. Long-time players have learned to expect bugs rather than be surprised by them.

Then there's the wider issue of EA's business practices. The franchise has increasingly felt focused on monetisation first and player experience second. The aggressive pack strategy, the endless stream of kits, and the perception that content is being drip-fed have left a sour taste for many veteran players.

And yet...

I've still played for over 900 hours.

Because underneath all the c…

DON'T BUY DLCS FOR THIS GAME!

Half of the content in the DLCs are completely broken and will not work, developers will never address or fix these bugs either.

The Sims 4 is an increasingly disappointing entry into a series of games that I've enjoyed for years. It's a buggy mess, held together by the player's patience and good-will (both of which I've run short of). It feels like every time the Devs touch it they break something else. 

For a while I got by making Sims and building (props where they're due, this game does those things well) but the game-play is shallow, glitchy and to me boring. 

The Sims franchise has always been on the pricey side, which is not and has never been great. But the Sims 4 takes price-gouging to an Olympic sports level. Asking for more and more money for less and less product. Product that is often busted and sometimes completely unplayable. 

I WANT to like this game, I WANT to want to play it... but I don't

'Play for free' but it takes a bit of my sanity away every time I open this game. What started as a very cool game, ends like a biggest disappointment to me. I have over 1k hours spent on building and playing, and I always end up losing the complete save due to bugs (even without mods). And yet, EA is still tossing around new packs and DLCs without fixing the age old existing bugs that prevent players from playing normally. 

Let me ask a question. If you keep expanding your game with new worlds and places for sims to visit, one can conclude that it has to be at least playable right? If I want to create a world with every place occupied, that should be doable, right? Well, sorry to disappoint, but after you spend hours in building and creating, the file corrupts and is not usable, all because the game can't handle it. THEN WHY GIVE US SO MANY DLCS. Also, before anyone starts blaming my game equipment, it runs games like baldurs gate 3 and spiderman fine. Not the issue. 

Man, I used to be happy to play the sims. Now I try and be disappointed to see my game STILL doesn't work. IT HAS BEEN 12 YEARS SINCE RELEASED. EA is the biggest money farmer I know. Shame.
